setupSteps: Clear a strip of floor about 1.8 m x 0.8 m (est.). Make sure nothing sharp is near your head or feet.
Lay the mat lengthwise. On a hard floor, add a folded towel under the upper back.
Lie on your back with your head on the mat. A thin folded towel under the head is fine if your neck feels strained, but not a thick pillow.
Bend both knees and put your feet flat on the floor.
Foot width: feet hip-width apart, toes pointing forward (NASM).

Foot distance: heels about 15–20 cm (6–8 inches) from your buttocks (NASM). A quick check: when you lift your hips, your shins should be close to vertical, with the knees above the ankles (NASM floor bridge: feet directly under the knees at the top). Some NHS sheets say "feet close to the buttocks".
Arms: lie them on the floor at your sides, palms down, about 30–45 degrees from your body (est.). They give light support; do not push hard through them.
Spine: let your lower back rest in its natural position. There may be a small gap under the lower back. Do not force it flat or arch it.
Head and eyes: look straight up at the ceiling. Do not turn the head while lifting.
Clothing: fitted track pants or leggings so you (and the camera) can see your hip and knee line.

steps.title: Press the feet into the floor
steps.action: Spread your weight evenly through each whole foot, like a tripod (big-toe joint, little-toe joint and heel). Keep the heels down.
steps.feel: Light pressure through the heels and the balls of the feet.
steps.visualCheck: Side: heels flat on the floor, toes not lifted. Front: feet hip-width, toes forward.

steps.title: Brace the stomach
steps.action: Gently tighten your stomach, as if you were about to cough. Do not suck it in hard.
steps.feel: A light firmness around the waist; your lower ribs stay down.
steps.visualCheck: Side: lower ribs do not flare up toward the ceiling.

steps.title: Squeeze the buttocks
steps.action: Squeeze your buttocks together before your hips leave the floor (NHS and NASM both cue the squeeze first).
steps.feel: Your buttocks tighten while you are still lying down.
steps.visualCheck: The pelvis may tilt very slightly (tail bone curls up a little); nothing else moves.

steps.title: Lift the hips
steps.action: Push through your feet and lift your hips off the floor until your body forms a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders (NASM).
steps.feel: The work is mostly in the buttocks, with some in the back of the thighs. No pinch in the lower back.
steps.breathing: Breathe out as you lift (Mayo Clinic).
steps.visualCheck: Side: straight line from knee to hip to shoulder; shins close to vertical; weight on the upper back and shoulders, not on the neck. Front: knees stay hip-width (not falling in or flaring out); hips level.

steps.title: Hold at the top
steps.action: Keep squeezing the buttocks. Do not push the hips higher than the straight line.
steps.feel: Strong squeeze in the buttocks; stomach lightly braced.
steps.breathing: Keep breathing; do not hold your breath. On longer holds, breathe slowly in and out.
steps.visualCheck: Side: hips do not sag below the line or rise above it (no arch in the lower back). Front: pelvis level, knees still in line with the feet.

steps.title: Lower with control
steps.action: Slowly lower your hips back to the floor, putting your back down from the upper back to the tail bone.
steps.feel: Buttocks still working as they control the lowering.
steps.visualCheck: No dropping or bouncing off the floor.

steps.title: Reset
steps.action: Let the buttocks touch the floor lightly, relax for a moment, check your feet have not slid away, then start the next rep.
steps.visualCheck: Feet still in the start spot.

steps.title: Lift into the two-leg bridge (steps 1–5 above)
Keeping the hips level, lift one foot a few centimetres off the floor, knee still bent. Feel the standing-side buttock work harder. Breathe out as the foot lifts. About 1–2 seconds
Put the foot back down. Breathe in
Repeat with the other foot. Visual check (front): the hips do not drop or twist toward the lifted leg
Lower the hips after the planned number of marches
From the setup position, straighten one leg (or lift it with the knee bent, pulled gently toward the chest, as in ACE's single-leg progression). Keep both thighs level with each other
Brace the stomach and squeeze the buttock on the side of the foot that is on the floor
Push through the heel on the floor and lift the hips until the line from the knee through the hip to the shoulder is straight. Breathe out. About 2 seconds
Hold 1–2 seconds. The pelvis must stay level (NHS: keep the pelvis "as level as possible"; no dropping or rotating)
Finish all reps on one side, then switch. Do the same number on each side

commonMistakes.title: Arching the lower back at the top (lifting too high)
commonMistakes.text: Arching the lower back at the top (lifting too high). Why: the lower back muscles take over and the joints at the back of the spine are pinched, while the buttocks do less. Fix: stop when the knee–hip–shoulder line is straight; keep the ribs down and buttocks squeezed. If you feel the lower back, lower a little.

commonMistakes.title: Hamstring cramp or doing it all with the back of the thigh
commonMistakes.text: Hamstring cramp or doing it all with the back of the thigh. Why: feet are usually too far from the buttocks, which makes the hamstrings do more (EMG shows hamstring activity rises as the knee straightens). Fix: walk the feet 2–5 cm (est.) closer and push through the heels. Some hamstring work is normal.

commonMistakes.title: Pushing through the toes (heels lifting)
commonMistakes.text: Pushing through the toes (heels lifting). Why: shifts work to the front of the thighs and calves. Fix: whole-foot tripod with heels heavy.

commonMistakes.title: Knees falling in or flaring out
commonMistakes.text: Knees falling in or flaring out. Why: reduces side-hip work and can strain the knees. Fix: knees over the second toe, hip-width; a cushion or rolled towel held lightly between the knees can help you feel the line (note: squeezing between the knees, hip adduction, increased hamstring and back activity in one Korean study, so keep the squeeze light).

commonMistakes.title: Rushing and bouncing the hips off the floor
commonMistakes.text: Rushing and bouncing the hips off the floor. Why: momentum does the work and the top squeeze is skipped. Fix: 2 seconds up, 1–2 seconds hold, 2–3 seconds down.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath. Why: breath-holding raises blood pressure (a concern for people with high blood pressure or heart disease). Fix: breathe out on the way up, in on the way down.

commonMistakes.title: Single-leg version: hips dropping or twisting toward the lifted leg
commonMistakes.text: Single-leg version: hips dropping or twisting toward the lifted leg. Why: the target side-hip muscles are not doing their job and the lower back twists. Fix: lower the hips a little, slow down, or go back to the marching bridge.

commonMistakes.title: Pushing with the arms or head
commonMistakes.text: Pushing with the arms or head. Why: strains the neck and shoulders and makes the hips work less. Fix: arms relaxed; eyes up.

safetyNotes: Lower back problems: usually included in physiotherapy back programmes, but lift only to a straight line, never into an arch, and use the small-range version during a flare-up. Stop if pain spreads down a leg.

Pregnancy: after the first trimester, ACOG-based guidance commonly advises avoiding exercises lying flat on the back, because the womb can press on the large blood vessels and cause dizziness or low blood pressure. Some sources describe short supine periods as acceptable if the person feels well. FitPlate default: avoid after the first trimester; swap to standing hip exercises (see section 13).

Postpartum: pelvic floor exercises can usually start early; bridges are a common gentle postnatal exercise, but get clearance from your midwife, GP or pelvic-health physiotherapist first, especially after a caesarean.
High blood pressure and heart disease: breathe continuously; avoid long, maximal-effort holds; get clearance if blood pressure is uncontrolled.
Neck problems: keep the weight on the upper back, not the neck; do not lift so high that the neck bends forward.
Recent hip, spine, abdominal or knee surgery: only with your surgeon's or physiotherapist's approval.
Hamstring injury: single-leg and feet-far versions load the hamstrings more; keep feet close and use the two-leg version.
